newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to sell $38 bln of securities next week. [CORRECTED 19:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. to sell $38 bln of securities next week. [CORRECTED 19:20 GMT]

text.p: The Treasury Department on Wednesday announced a $38-billion quarterly refunding to be held next week.
Treasury said next week's auctions will refund $26.8 billion of maturing securities and raise $11.2 billion of new cash.
The auctions will consist of $16 billion of three-year notes, $12 billion of 10-year notes and $10 billion of 30-year bonds.

Ahead of the refunding annoucement, there was speculation in financial markets that Treasury might eliminate some issues because of the steep and unexpected decline in the government's budget deficit and borrowing needs.
However, Deputy Assistant Treasury Secretary Roger Anderson said at a news conference that the department was not now considering eliminating any issues.
"We are not currently contemplating any further cycle changes," Anderson said in response to questions.
Asked if that meant that Treasury would make no further changes in its auction cycle this year, Anderson replied, "We like to announce changes ahead of time. We're not thinking of any now."

In its recommendations to the department, the private-sector Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee said it would be better to reduce the size of future offerings rather than to eliminate some maturities.
"The committee members felt that existing note offerings, particularly out to five years, as well as existing bill offerings could be adjusted," the panel's report said.

The panel, however, warned that there were "practical limitations" to how far the weekly bill offerings could be reduced without hurting the market's liquidity. But it added that this was not a "current concern" given recent increases in the weekly bill auctions.

The panel also suggested that Treasury make all fixed-rate notes eligible for stripping. Currently, only securities with a maturity of 10 years or more can be sold with the coupons stripped from the principal of the security.
"We are in the process of evaluating this proposal and its potential value to market participants," Anderson said.
Anderson repeated Treasury's commitment to development of the inflation-indexed securities market and said the department was pleased at the reception of the last auction of five-year notes.

Anderson said that Treasury plans to reopen the five-year note in October and sell a new 10-year indexed security in January. It also plans a 30-year indexed bond next year but the exact timing has not yet been set.
After a strong start, sales of the indexed securities have slowed as inflation fears have ebbed.

Anderson said that Treasury will issue final rules soon to implement half-decimal bidding for bill auctions and to reduce the threshhold for reporting net long bill positions to $1 billion from $2 billion.
He said Treasury will give market participants adequate time to prepare for the changes.
At next week's quarterly refunding, Treasury will offer three-year notes on Tuesday, 10-year notes on Wednesday and 30-year bonds on Thursday.

After next week's refunding auctions, Treasury will need to pay down $2 billion in market borrowings during the rest of the third quarter. That can be done through regular sales of three- and six-month and one-year bills, and two- and five-year notes in August and September.
"Another cash management bill, in addition to the one announced (on Tuesday), may be needed to cover the low point in the cash balance in early September," Anderson said.
Treasury said on Tuesday it will sell $18 billion of 48-day cash management bills on July 31. (Corrects date from Aug 1 to July 31.)
As previously reported, the Treasury estimates its net market borrowing requirement in the October-December fourth quarter will be $45-50 billion, assuming a $30-billion cash balance on Dec 31.
-- Washington newsroom, ((202-898-8300))
